zh-Hans.s6.SGP.visit.c: 说清现在的限度，暂不约定
zh-Hans.s6.SGP.visit.c.result: 你告诉{person}现在还不能安排时间，没有许下不确定的日期。那个家中故事仍是一张便条，没有变成已经完成的相处。
zh-Hans.s6.SGP.visit.c.follow: 后来，你重读便条，也记得当时为什么没有约定。记录没有补上一场未发生的相处，也没有惩罚你当时需要的限度。
zh-Hans.s6.SGP.visit.c.later: 几年后，那份没有约定的计划，仍和确实相处过的时间分得开。你可以同时留着感谢，也留着一个没答完的问题。

en.s6.daily.childhood.1: Rain taps the window. You move a finger beside one drop and follow it to the sill.
en.s6.daily.childhood.2: You build a room from cushions. The doorway is just wide enough for your favorite toy.
en.s6.daily.childhood.3: Your shadow stretches across the ground. You change your steps to see it move.
en.s6.daily.childhood.4: You fill a page with color. One mark goes beyond the edge, and you make it part of the picture.
en.s6.daily.childhood.5: A familiar tune begins nearby. You join in with the part you recognize.
en.s6.daily.childhood.6: You give a toy a name. When you put it away, you say the name once more.
en.s6.daily.childhood.7: A seed has opened in a small pot. You bring it closer to the light.
en.s6.daily.childhood.8: An empty box becomes a vehicle in your game. Its first journey stays inside the room.
en.s6.daily.childhood.9: You sort a few belongings into places of your own. Finding them later feels a little easier.
en.s6.daily.childhood.10: You compare a leaf with a smooth stone. You keep noticing how different they feel.
en.s6.daily.childhood.11: You pause by an open doorway. A sound outside becomes something you want to ask about.
en.s6.daily.childhood.12: At a meal you try an unfamiliar flavor. You take time to decide whether you like it.
en.s6.daily.childhood.13: A small fastening takes several tries. This time your hands find where it belongs.
en.s6.daily.childhood.14: You collect a few small treasures in a box. Each has a reason that matters to you.
en.s6.daily.childhood.15: You invent an adventure using things within reach. You decide where this part of the story ends.
en.s6.daily.childhood.16: Evening changes the color of the room. You watch one bright patch become softer.
en.s6.daily.childhood.17: You choose a quiet corner to sit in. For a little while, watching is enough.
en.s6.daily.childhood.18: You arrange small objects in a pattern. One space is left for the next thing you might find.
en.s6.daily.childhood.19: You try a small task again after getting it wrong. This attempt works differently from the first.
en.s6.daily.childhood.20: You put one ordinary object somewhere safe. For today, it is the thing you want to keep.
en.s6.daily.study.1: A question stays with you after class. You mark the place instead of pretending you understood it.
en.s6.daily.study.2: You explain part of a lesson in your own words. A confusing sentence becomes a little clearer.
en.s6.daily.study.3: You return to a page you once skipped. You recognize one step that used to stop you.
en.s6.daily.study.4: You write a short study plan. There is space beside it for changing your mind after trying.
en.s6.daily.study.5: One topic keeps drawing you back to a book. You read a little beyond the assigned page.
en.s6.daily.study.6: A borrowed book shows you a useful method. You try it before deciding whether it suits you.
en.s6.daily.study.7: You ask about a step you did not understand. Saying it aloud takes more courage than writing a note.
en.s6.daily.study.8: You make a small example with your hands. The idea becomes easier to see outside the textbook.
en.s6.daily.study.9: You keep a little time for a difficult exercise. You finish one part and mark the rest for later.
en.s6.daily.study.10: You compare two explanations of the same idea. You write down where they differ.
en.s6.daily.study.11: You notice a mistake in an earlier answer. You correct the step without tearing up the whole page.
en.s6.daily.study.12: You choose one example to review before a test. Doing a small part carefully steadies the rest of the hour.
en.s6.daily.study.13: A lesson takes longer than you expected. You leave a note about where to begin next time.
en.s6.daily.study.14: You use an everyday object to understand a lesson. The object becomes a reminder of how you learned it.
en.s6.daily.study.15: You gather scattered notes into one place. One unfinished question gets its own heading.
en.s6.daily.study.16: You practice a part that once felt impossible. Today it is still slow, but no longer unfamiliar.
en.s6.daily.study.17: You look back at an early exercise. You can point to one thing you would now do differently.
en.s6.daily.study.18: You stop copying an explanation word for word. Your own rough version says more about what you understand.
en.s6.daily.study.19: You finish a shared classroom task. You keep a note of the part you contributed.
en.s6.daily.study.20: You put a completed exercise beside an unfinished one. Both belong to the same period of learning.
en.s6.daily.friendship.1: You and {person} talk after a shared task. A small detail becomes a joke you both recognize.
en.s6.daily.friendship.2: {person} asks about something you mentioned earlier. You are surprised that the detail was remembered.
en.s6.daily.friendship.3: You and {person} spend a quiet part of the day together. Neither has to fill every pause.
en.s6.daily.friendship.4: You show {person} an unfinished attempt. The conversation stays with the attempt instead of a score.
en.s6.daily.friendship.5: {person} tells you about a difficult small task. You listen without having a ready answer.
en.s6.daily.friendship.6: You and {person} remember the first task you did together. You disagree about one harmless detail.
en.s6.daily.friendship.7: You save a note from {person}. It is ordinary enough that someone else might have thrown it away.
en.s6.daily.friendship.8: You ask {person} a question you had kept to yourself. The answer opens a different part of the conversation.
en.s6.daily.friendship.9: You and {person} make a small shared plan. You write it down as a plan, with room for either person to change it.
en.s6.daily.friendship.10: You explain a boundary to {person}. A friendship can include saying what does not work for you.
en.s6.daily.friendship.11: {person} shares a small success. You ask how it happened instead of comparing it with your own progress.
en.s6.daily.friendship.12: You and {person} exchange practical help. You keep track of what happened without turning it into a debt.
en.s6.daily.friendship.13: You notice that your interests and {person}'s are different. You find one small thing you can still talk about.
en.s6.daily.friendship.14: You and {person} revisit a shared mistake. It is easier to speak about it with some time between you and that day.
en.s6.daily.friendship.15: You keep a brief greeting from {person}. Not every contact has to become a long conversation.
en.s6.daily.friendship.16: You and {person} finish a conversation without solving everything. You both know which part is still open.
en.s6.daily.friendship.17: {person} asks for a little space. You leave the next message unsent for now.
en.s6.daily.friendship.18: You return something you borrowed from {person}. A small thank-you stays attached to an ordinary errand.
en.s6.daily.friendship.19: You and {person} share a memory from before your lives changed. It does not require either life to return to that time.
en.s6.daily.friendship.20: You write down one thing you learned from knowing {person}. It is specific to this connection, not a rule about everyone.
en.s6.daily.family.1: You and {person} share an ordinary meal. One remark stays with you after the dishes are put away.
en.s6.daily.family.2: {person} shows you an old object. You ask which part of its story they want to tell.
en.s6.daily.family.3: You and {person} do a small household task together. Being useful is only one part of spending time nearby.
en.s6.daily.family.4: You listen to a familiar story from {person}. This time you notice a detail you had missed.
en.s6.daily.family.5: You tell {person} about an ordinary part of your day. There is no announcement, only something shared.
en.s6.daily.family.6: You and {person} arrange a shared space. You leave room for both of your preferences.
en.s6.daily.family.7: {person} asks what would help with a small task. You answer plainly instead of hoping it will be guessed.
en.s6.daily.family.8: You and {person} look at something kept from earlier years. You name one moment you both recognize.
en.s6.daily.family.9: You ask {person} about a routine you had never questioned. The answer gives it a small history.
en.s6.daily.family.10: You and {person} disagree about a small arrangement. You name the practical problem without deciding the whole relationship by it.
en.s6.daily.family.11: You say thank you to {person} for something specific. The reason matters more than a perfect sentence.
en.s6.daily.family.12: {person} mentions a preference you did not know. You keep it in mind for a later conversation.
en.s6.daily.family.13: You and {person} finish part of an unfinished task. You stop before turning an ordinary day into a deadline.
en.s6.daily.family.14: You sit nearby while {person} does something familiar. You notice how much of knowing a person happens quietly.
en.s6.daily.family.15: You and {person} decide what can wait. Leaving one thing undone gives the rest of the day more room.
en.s6.daily.family.16: {person} asks about an earlier choice of yours. You explain what you knew at the time.
en.s6.daily.family.17: You and {person} keep a small shared object. You remember what was happening when it first mattered.
en.s6.daily.family.18: You share a quiet pause with {person}. It does not need to become a lesson or a photograph.
en.s6.daily.family.19: You tell {person} what you can and cannot arrange this time. A clear answer replaces an uncertain promise.
en.s6.daily.family.20: You keep a detail from a conversation with {person}. The memory has a person attached to it, not only an age.
en.s6.daily.work.1: A task is returned with one practical question. You clarify the question before starting the work again.
en.s6.daily.work.2: You finish a small part of a larger task. You mark what is complete instead of claiming the whole project is done.
en.s6.daily.work.3: You ask for the information a task needs. The request takes a little courage but prevents more guessing.
en.s6.daily.work.4: A familiar method stops working well. You test one small change before replacing everything.
en.s6.daily.work.5: You explain an unfinished piece of work clearly. Naming what remains makes the next step easier to arrange.
en.s6.daily.work.6: You keep a useful note from a difficult task. It records a method, not a promise that every problem will be easy.
en.s6.daily.work.7: You notice one repeated inconvenience at work. You write down a possible improvement and its limits.
en.s6.daily.work.8: You ask which part of a request matters most. A shorter answer changes how you use the remaining time.
en.s6.daily.work.9: You acknowledge a mistake in a work task. You describe what you can correct without making an unlimited promise.
en.s6.daily.work.10: You finish the work you agreed to do. You leave a clear handover for the part that belongs to another task.
en.s6.daily.work.11: You learn a small practical skill during a task. Its value is visible in one thing that now takes less effort.
en.s6.daily.work.12: You compare the estimate with how long a task actually took. You leave a more honest note for next time.
en.s6.daily.work.13: You put a boundary around an extra request. Saying what fits makes the help more definite.
en.s6.daily.work.14: You revisit an early piece of your work. You can recognize both what you learned and what was difficult then.
en.s6.daily.work.15: You prepare one question before a work conversation. It helps you ask for something more specific than approval.
en.s6.daily.work.16: You divide a task into smaller parts. One part can begin even though the full plan is not settled.
en.s6.daily.work.17: You write down who needs which information. An ordinary clarification prevents a needless round of work.
en.s6.daily.work.18: You complete a repair to a routine process. You keep a note of what changed and what did not.
en.s6.daily.work.19: You end a work conversation with an agreed next step. It is a commitment of a known size.
en.s6.daily.work.20: You put away the materials at the end of a task. You allow a finished part to be finished for today.
en.s6.daily.home.1: You move one everyday object to a better place. The room begins to work a little more easily for you.
en.s6.daily.home.2: You prepare something simple for yourself. Paying attention to the small process changes how the pause feels.
en.s6.daily.home.3: You sort a drawer and keep one unexpected object. You can say why it still belongs here.
en.s6.daily.home.4: You leave one part of the day unplanned. You use it without having to turn it into an achievement.
en.s6.daily.home.5: You repair a small inconvenience at home. It changes a repeated moment rather than the whole of life.
en.s6.daily.home.6: You choose a place for something you want to remember. Seeing it becomes a quiet part of the room.
en.s6.daily.home.7: You try a different route through an ordinary day. You notice one thing the usual routine missed.
en.s6.daily.home.8: You put an unfinished task where you can return to it. It does not have to occupy the whole room.
en.s6.daily.home.9: You keep a small ritual that is yours. Today you do it without asking it to solve everything.
en.s6.daily.home.10: You compare what you use with what you only keep moving around. One small decision makes the space clearer.
en.s6.daily.home.11: You take time over an ordinary meal. For a while, it is allowed to be the main thing you are doing.
en.s6.daily.home.12: You open a window or move toward the light. You notice the room before returning to the next task.
en.s6.daily.home.13: You label a box you had meant to sort. Naming what is inside becomes a manageable beginning.
en.s6.daily.home.14: You choose which small task can wait. Keeping a limit makes room for the rest of the day.
en.s6.daily.home.15: You return to an object you once set aside. You decide where it fits in the life you have now.
en.s6.daily.home.16: You notice a sound that belongs to an ordinary day. Later you want to keep the scene, not only the task.
en.s6.daily.home.17: You finish one small repair without replacing everything around it. Enough can be a practical decision.
en.s6.daily.home.18: You make a little space for something you enjoy. It remains a part of the room even when no one sees it.
en.s6.daily.home.19: You put a useful note somewhere visible. An ordinary reminder makes one return to a task easier.
en.s6.daily.home.20: You end a quiet part of the day by putting one thing away. The small ending feels complete enough.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.1: You notice that you need a pause and take one. You record a rest, not a promise about future health.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.2: You leave a small gap between two tasks. The next thing does not have to begin immediately.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.3: You choose an easier version of a planned activity. Adjusting it lets you take part at your own pace.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.4: You notice where a routine has become uncomfortable. You make one practical adjustment and see how it feels.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.5: You put a difficult task down for a while. You leave a note about returning instead of forcing a conclusion.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.6: You spend a quiet interval without adding another obligation. The pause does not need to be productive.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.7: You pay attention to how an activity feels today. You adjust the plan rather than comparing with another day.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.8: You choose one manageable thing from a long list. Completing it does not make the rest disappear, but gives you a place to stop.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.9: You take a short walk or move gently within the space available. You notice something beyond the task you were doing.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.10: You make a plan smaller after noticing your limits. The revised plan belongs to the day you actually have.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.11: You leave an unfinished question unanswered for now. You can keep the question without carrying it through every task.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.12: You choose a quieter setting for a little while. You return to the day after giving the pause some room.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.13: You notice one source of unnecessary hurry. Removing a small deadline changes the next part of the day.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.14: You make it easier to begin a routine task. Moving one object can be more useful than demanding more willpower.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.15: You pause before accepting another optional task. You check what you already agreed to do.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.16: You take care of a simple need before another task. For today, that order makes sense.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.17: You notice the difference between a difficult day and a judgment about your whole life. You record the day as it was.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.18: You try an activity in a gentler way. Choosing a limit lets it remain something you can return to.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.19: You stop measuring one quiet interval by what you achieved. You keep one detail of what you noticed instead.
en.s6.daily.wellbeing.20: You choose a stopping point before you are completely worn out. One task remains for another day.
en.s6.daily.reflection.1: You open an earlier record from this life. Knowing what came later does not erase what you knew then.
en.s6.daily.reflection.2: You keep an ordinary moment beside a major turning point. Both took real space in the life you lived.
en.s6.daily.reflection.3: You revisit a choice that did not resolve everything. You can name what it did change.
en.s6.daily.reflection.4: You find a record of an unfinished plan. You keep the unfinished part instead of inventing a conclusion.
en.s6.daily.reflection.5: You place an earlier attempt beside a later one. The difference is more specific than success or failure.
en.s6.daily.reflection.6: You reread a moment you chose to keep. One small detail still tells you why it mattered.
en.s6.daily.reflection.7: You look at a path you actually followed. You leave the unchosen alternatives open rather than claiming to know their endings.
en.s6.daily.reflection.8: You keep a note about what was uncertain at the time. It makes an old decision easier to understand.
en.s6.daily.reflection.9: You find an ordinary object connected with an earlier record. The scene returns before any lesson does.
en.s6.daily.reflection.10: You put two different feelings about an old chapter into words. They do not have to cancel each other.
en.s6.daily.reflection.11: You choose not to turn an old memory into advice. It can remain one person's experience.
en.s6.daily.reflection.12: You read a record of a small beginning. The later result does not make the first step inevitable.
en.s6.daily.reflection.13: You find a detail that never appeared in a score. You decide it still belongs in the story.
en.s6.daily.reflection.14: You keep a changed plan beside the original one. Adapting was part of what actually happened.
en.s6.daily.reflection.15: You notice a gap in the record. You leave it visible instead of filling it with a story you cannot support.
en.s6.daily.reflection.16: You revisit the reason behind an earlier boundary. The limit made sense in a particular part of life.
en.s6.daily.reflection.17: You choose a small scene as a first page. You do not ask it to explain every chapter that followed.
en.s6.daily.reflection.18: You keep an old question alongside a later answer. The distance between them belongs to the story too.
en.s6.daily.reflection.19: You read an earlier chapter without rushing to rewrite it. Understanding can be different from correcting.
en.s6.daily.reflection.20: You gather a few recorded moments into one place. What you keep is this particular life, with its open questions.
en.s6.local.CHN.1: You find a handwritten comment inside a borrowed book. For once, the page feels like a conversation.
en.s6.local.CHN.2: You stop at a cultural center noticeboard. A beginner activity catches your eye; you copy down the contact details without committing yet.
en.s6.local.CHN.3: You and {person} sort photographs at a table. The name on one photograph takes longer to remember than the occasion.
en.s6.local.CHN.4: On the way home, {person} waits while you finish a story. This time, nobody hurries to give advice.
en.s6.local.CHN.5: You keep a note for a small project you might try after work. Today, keeping the idea is enough.
en.s6.local.CHN.6: You make a tiny stage from a cardboard box. The first audience is a row of toys.
en.s6.local.CHN.7: You choose a quieter route after a crowded afternoon. Nothing is achieved; you arrive home less tense.
en.s6.local.CHN.8: At home you mend the loose corner of a notebook. You keep the old cover instead of replacing it.
en.s6.local.CHN.9: A familiar tune brings back an ordinary room from earlier life. You remember its light more clearly than its furniture.
en.s6.local.CHN.10: {person} tells you how an everyday object came into the household. You had seen it for years without knowing the story.
en.s6.local.JPN.1: You stay a moment longer at the school library shelf. A thin book contains an idea you want to try for yourself.
en.s6.local.JPN.2: A kominkan notice lists beginner learning activities. You mark one that allows people to start without bringing finished work.
en.s6.local.JPN.3: You and {person} label a box of mementos. Some descriptions are only a few words, but you recognize the handwriting.
en.s6.local.JPN.4: {person} shows you a penciled note from school. You disagree about one detail and enjoy remembering it differently.
en.s6.local.JPN.5: You put away work materials and leave a small cleared space for something of your own.
en.s6.local.JPN.6: You fold paper into something that will not quite stand up. You make a second base instead of starting over.
en.s6.local.JPN.7: You sit beside an open window and let a quiet part of the day stay quiet.
en.s6.local.JPN.8: An old cloth becomes a cover for a notebook. The uneven seam makes it easy to recognize.
en.s6.local.JPN.9: You remember the walk after an ordinary lesson. It was not a milestone, yet the route has stayed with you.
en.s6.local.JPN.10: {person} asks which small object you would keep. You choose one whose story you can actually tell.
en.s6.local.IND.1: At a school reading activity, you hear the same passage explained in different words. One version finally makes sense to you.
en.s6.local.IND.2: A reading group invitation leaves room for more than one language. You note an activity without deciding what language you will use.
en.s6.local.IND.3: You ask {person} to repeat a phrase used at home. Writing it down takes more patience than you expected.
en.s6.local.IND.4: You and {person} remember a story read at school. Each of you remembers a different character most clearly.
en.s6.local.IND.5: After work, you find an old page of ideas. You choose one line to keep visible instead of turning it into another task list.
en.s6.local.IND.6: You tell a picture-book story using your own words. The pictures stay the same; your version changes at every telling.
en.s6.local.IND.7: You take a short break from answering questions. There is room for one question of your own.
en.s6.local.IND.8: You sew a loose button back onto a bag. A familiar object gets another ordinary day.
en.s6.local.IND.9: You read a note in a language you once practiced. Some words take time to return; you let them.
en.s6.local.IND.10: {person} tells a familiar story but changes the ending this time. You ask what made the difference.
en.s6.local.USA.1: A school project leaves you with a rough sketch instead of a finished answer. You keep the sketch after the assignment ends.
en.s6.local.USA.2: You read the beginner instructions for a library creative workshop. You note that joining would take planning, not special talent.
en.s6.local.USA.3: You and {person} record the story behind a photograph. A pause in the recording becomes part of the story.
en.s6.local.USA.4: {person} remembers a school presentation you thought everyone had forgotten. The remembered detail is kindly specific.
en.s6.local.USA.5: You decline one optional task and spend the cleared time on a small unfinished project at home.
en.s6.local.USA.6: You make a neighborhood out of blocks. A crooked little building becomes the place your toys keep returning to.
en.s6.local.USA.7: You walk without tracking a distance. At the end, you remember a tree rather than a number.
en.s6.local.USA.8: You make a small repair using instructions from a borrowed book. You check each step instead of pretending you already know.
en.s6.local.USA.9: An old project file contains an early mistake. You keep it beside the improved version rather than deleting the evidence of learning.
en.s6.local.USA.10: {person} asks to hear a memory you usually leave out. You tell the ordinary part first.
en.s6.local.BRA.1: Your class makes a display together. One small piece of your work stays in the corner where you can recognize it.
en.s6.local.BRA.2: A community culture group displays work in progress. You find the unfinished pieces easier to approach than the polished ones.
en.s6.local.BRA.3: You and {person} write names beside a family photograph. An unknown face remains an honest blank.
en.s6.local.BRA.4: {person} recalls the classroom display you made together. You laugh about the part held up by too much tape.
en.s6.local.BRA.5: You save a little time after work for a creative idea. You do not need to make it profitable for it to belong in your day.
en.s6.local.BRA.6: You turn an empty package into a pretend shop. The first thing you trade is a made-up story.
en.s6.local.BRA.7: You sit outside for a little while and notice a familiar sound you had stopped hearing.
en.s6.local.BRA.8: You rearrange a small corner to make room for your notebook. The room has not grown, but one idea now has a place.
en.s6.local.BRA.9: A page from an old creative notebook surprises you. You like a detail your earlier self did not seem to value.
en.s6.local.BRA.10: {person} remembers who took the photograph. For a moment you talk about the person behind the camera, too.
en.s6.local.NGA.1: At a classroom reading, you volunteer one sentence. The voice is yours even when the words belong to the book.
en.s6.local.NGA.2: You read a library activity leaflet. One session invites people to bring a story they remember, rather than a finished essay.
en.s6.local.NGA.3: You write down a story as {person} tells it. You ask to keep a particular turn of phrase instead of replacing it with your own.
en.s6.local.NGA.4: {person} remembers a classroom reading you practiced together. You try one line again and both lose your place.
en.s6.local.NGA.5: You find a library leaflet inside your work notebook. You leave it there as a possibility, not another obligation.
en.s6.local.NGA.6: You give your toys different voices. One soft-spoken character gets the last word for once.
en.s6.local.NGA.7: You put a busy conversation aside and listen to the quiet around you. A short pause changes the rest of the evening.
en.s6.local.NGA.8: You protect the cover of a well-used book. The marks inside remain part of its history.
en.s6.local.NGA.9: You reread a sentence copied years earlier. You no longer agree with all of it, but remember why you kept it.
en.s6.local.NGA.10: {person} asks you to tell the story back. You check a detail instead of confidently inventing it.
en.s6.local.FRA.1: A borrowed library book has room for more than one interpretation. You write your own question on a separate slip rather than searching for the expected answer.
en.s6.local.FRA.2: On a municipal library shelf, you find a book about an amateur art you once wanted to try. You copy down its title, not a promise to become good at it.
en.s6.local.FRA.3: You and {person} compare two dates on the back of a family photograph. A small disagreement turns into a story about that afternoon.
en.s6.local.FRA.4: {person} remembers the uneven lettering on a school display. You had remembered the nervousness; they had remembered your careful work.
en.s6.local.FRA.5: An arts activity leaflet stays under your work notebook for a week. You finally move it to the page where you keep ideas that belong to you.
en.s6.local.FRA.6: You draw a small map of a place you know. A doorway becomes much bigger on paper because it matters to your story.
en.s6.local.FRA.7: You take a book outside but read only two pages. Watching the light change is part of the afternoon, too.
en.s6.local.FRA.8: You repair a torn corner of a library-book note. The remembered idea matters more than keeping the paper perfect.
en.s6.local.FRA.9: An old activity leaflet contains a question you used to avoid: what would you make if it did not have to impress anyone? You read it more slowly now.
en.s6.local.FRA.10: {person} explains why an ordinary photograph was kept. The reason is smaller, and more personal, than the occasion written on its back.
en.s6.local.TWN.1: You find a classroom journal page in your school things. The neat heading and the crossed-out first sentence show two sides of the same attempt.
en.s6.local.TWN.2: A public library craft reading group shows how a book can become something made by hand. You note one beginner idea that would fit the materials you already have.
en.s6.local.TWN.3: Rain keeps you and {person} beside an old album for a little longer. You ask about the photograph usually passed over without comment.
en.s6.local.TWN.4: {person} recalls a sentence from the classroom journal you made together. Neither of you remembers who first suggested it, and that no longer seems important.
en.s6.local.TWN.5: After a full day, you put a bookmarked craft book beside your work bag. You have not started the project; you have made it easier to find again.
en.s6.local.TWN.6: You keep a paper boat on a dry windowsill instead of putting it into the rain. It can be an adventure even before it goes anywhere.
en.s6.local.TWN.7: You wait for a shower to pass without filling the pause with another task. A few unclaimed minutes become your own.
en.s6.local.TWN.8: You sew a small pocket inside a well-used bag. An old object now has a place for the notebook you keep carrying.
en.s6.local.TWN.9: An old journal page preserves a worry that has grown smaller with time. You remember its importance then without laughing at yourself.
en.s6.local.TWN.10: {person} remembers the person who stood just outside the photograph. You leave a note for the story the picture alone could not show.
en.s6.local.HKG.1: At a public library reading display, one question makes you stop: which part of a story would you tell in your own words? You try a sentence in your notebook.
en.s6.local.HKG.2: You find a creative idea in the margin of a small reading notebook. The library book that prompted it is gone, but your unfinished sentence is still there.
en.s6.local.HKG.3: You and {person} compare a photograph with the names written on its back. One place has changed, while a small detail in the story has not.
en.s6.local.HKG.4: {person} remembers a pause in the classroom reading you practiced together. What felt like a mistake to you had given them time to follow.
en.s6.local.HKG.5: You put the reading notebook beside your work papers and add one line that is not meant for a deadline. It changes the feeling of the desk.
en.s6.local.HKG.6: You build a little room inside a cardboard box. There is space for a toy, a window, and something you have not decided yet.
en.s6.local.HKG.7: You sit down with a book after a crowded journey. For a few pages, you do not have to keep moving.
en.s6.local.HKG.8: You change the label on an old storage box. Finding the notebook inside next time will take less searching.
en.s6.local.HKG.9: A note about an old place brings back an ordinary walk. You remember whom you talked with more clearly than the route you took.
en.s6.local.HKG.10: {person} notices a word you wrote differently on the back of a photograph. You ask how they would tell the story instead of deciding which version wins.
en.s6.local.SGP.1: Your school group project leaves an unused sketch. You keep it because the discarded idea still makes you curious.
en.s6.local.SGP.2: Introductory material from a library creative space shows a small project in stages. You notice that the unfinished middle is part of learning, too.
en.s6.local.SGP.3: You write down {person}'s explanation of a family photograph. You keep the familiar phrasing instead of polishing away their voice.
en.s6.local.SGP.4: {person} remembers the school project sketch you did not use. You compare what each of you would keep from it now.
en.s6.local.SGP.5: You find a making leaflet between two work documents. You leave one possible evening beside it rather than committing every week.
en.s6.local.SGP.6: You build two different bridges for the same toy. One falls over, and you keep the pieces for another version.
en.s6.local.SGP.7: You pause under shelter while rain passes. Watching a few drops collect becomes a small part of the day you can remember clearly.
en.s6.local.SGP.8: You sort a few reusable materials into a small box. A future project gets a starting point without taking over the whole room.
en.s6.local.SGP.9: An introductory leaflet reminds you how much a first attempt can ask of someone. You are kinder to the early sketch you once hid.
en.s6.local.SGP.10: {person} asks you to repeat a photograph's story. You check one uncertain detail and leave another question for a later conversation.
en.s6.small-courage.prompt: The pieces are still on the table. Someone nearby can help, but you also want to see what your own hands can do. Where will you begin?
en.s6.small-courage.preludeTitle: A toy you tried to mend
en.s6.small-courage.setup: A favorite toy has come apart. You keep its pieces together instead of throwing them away.
en.s6.small-courage.a.result: You try several arrangements and keep the pieces that fit. The toy is not perfect, but part of the repair is yours.
en.s6.small-courage.a.follow: When a small task goes wrong later, you remember that trying slowly can be a beginning.
en.s6.small-courage.b: Ask someone to work beside me
en.s6.small-courage.b.result: You ask for help and hold a piece while the other person shows you where it goes.
en.s6.small-courage.b.follow: You keep a memory of being helped without having to hide what you did not know.
en.s6.small-courage.c: Keep it safely and return another day
en.s6.small-courage.c.result: You place the pieces in a box. Today you choose another game; the unfinished toy is still yours.
en.s6.small-courage.c.follow: You find the box again. You can keep an unfinished thing without judging the whole day by it.
en.s6.school-friend.prompt: {person} is alone during a break. You recognize the person who laughed with you earlier. What would feel possible today?
en.s6.school-friend.preludeTitle: The person at the next desk
en.s6.school-friend.setup: You and {person} work on the same classroom task. A shared mistake makes both of you laugh.
en.s6.school-friend.a.result: You make room in the game and explain the rules. Joining takes a little time, but you start together.
en.s6.school-friend.a.follow: You and {person} recognize one another more easily now; that first invitation has become a shared memory.
en.s6.school-friend.b: Sit nearby and start with one question
en.s6.school-friend.b.result: You sit nearby and ask about the classroom task. A short answer becomes a short conversation.
en.s6.school-friend.b.follow: You and {person} sometimes begin a conversation with that same ordinary question.
en.s6.school-friend.c: Offer a greeting and keep some space
en.s6.school-friend.c.result: You greet {person} and leave the nearby seat free. Today there is no longer conversation.
en.s6.school-friend.c.follow: You still recognize {person}. A greeting can remain a greeting, without a friendship being owed.
en.s6.first-interest: Something you want to take seriously
en.s6.first-interest.prompt: An informal activity gives you a place to share {interest}. Other plans already fill some of your time. How much room do you want to make?
en.s6.first-interest.preludeTitle: A page that was not homework
en.s6.first-interest.setup: You begin {interest} in a spare part of the day. There is no grade for it, and you return to it once more.
en.s6.first-interest.a.result: You reserve a small part of your week for {interest}. Another leisure activity gets less time for now.
en.s6.first-interest.a.follow: You have a few pieces of practice to look back on. Your interest has a place in the week, even without a prize.
en.s6.first-interest.b.result: You bring one unfinished attempt to the activity. You listen to a response without promising to make this your whole life.
en.s6.first-interest.b.follow: You remember being seen while you were still learning. That response stays with your early work.
en.s6.first-interest.c.result: You keep {interest} in your own notebook and keep the current plans. The activity passes without you.
en.s6.first-interest.c.follow: You find your early notebook again. Keeping something private was also a choice you made.
en.s6.words-at-home.prompt: {person} asks how things have been. You remember the conversation you stopped halfway. What would you like to share this time?
en.s6.words-at-home.setup: While talking with {person}, you stop just before saying what you have been thinking about your next chapter.
en.s6.words-at-home.a: Say what I hope for, even if it is uncertain
en.s6.words-at-home.a.result: You tell {person} one hope and one uncertainty. There is no instant agreement, but the words have been heard.
en.s6.words-at-home.a.follow: A later conversation with {person} has somewhere to begin: you can refer to what you said instead of starting from silence.
en.s6.words-at-home.b: Ask about them, then share one small thing
en.s6.words-at-home.b.result: You ask about {person}, then share one small part of your own life. You leave the larger question open.
en.s6.words-at-home.b.follow: You and {person} have one more ordinary thing to ask about when you next speak.
en.s6.words-at-home.c.result: You write the rest of the sentence for yourself. It is not sent, and you do not count it as a conversation.
en.s6.words-at-home.c.follow: The unsent page helps you see what you meant. Whether to share it remains your decision.
en.s6.old-friend: What if you sent one honest sentence?
en.s6.old-friend.prompt: You and {person} shared a real school memory, then lived separate years. An answer is not guaranteed. What kind of contact would you be comfortable offering?
en.s6.old-friend.preludeTitle: A name from a different chapter
en.s6.old-friend.setup: You find a trace of school and remember {person}. The last recorded contact was at age {lastAge}. You wonder what you would say now, without assuming they have been waiting.
en.s6.old-friend.a: Send a memory, with no demand for a reply
en.s6.old-friend.a.result: You send {person} one specific school memory and say there is no hurry to answer. You leave space for a life you do not know about.
en.s6.old-friend.a.follow: A short reply arrives from {person}, adding a detail you forgot. You exchange a little news; a renewed conversation is not a promise to recover every lost year.
en.s6.old-friend.a.later: Years later, you reread those few messages. You did not become inseparable, but you now know that the old memory belonged to both of you.
en.s6.old-friend.b: Ask whether a short catch-up would suit them
en.s6.old-friend.b.result: You ask {person} whether a short catch-up would fit their schedule and suggest that another time, or no meeting, is fine.
en.s6.old-friend.b.follow: You find a short time that suits you both. The conversation has a few silences; you hear one part of the years you did not share.
en.s6.old-friend.b.later: Years later, one detail from that catch-up comes back to you. You remember asking rather than assuming there was still room for the old friendship.
en.s6.old-friend.c: Keep the memory without contacting them now
en.s6.old-friend.c.result: You write down what you remember and do not send a message today. You do not decide how {person} would have answered.
en.s6.old-friend.c.follow: You find the note again. It contains a memory, not evidence that a conversation or reunion took place.
en.s6.old-friend.c.later: Years later, you still cannot know what a message would have changed. You let the friendship matter without giving its unfinished part an invented ending.
en.s6.return-interest: If nobody graded it, would you begin again?
en.s6.return-interest.prompt: An invitation has made you think about {interest} again. Work still takes time, and starting over may feel awkward. What can you honestly make room for?
en.s6.return-interest.preludeTitle: The part of you that waited
en.s6.return-interest.setup: While sorting your things, you find the materials for {interest}. You remember putting them away when work began. You leave one piece on the table tonight.
en.s6.return-interest.a: Reserve one small session for myself
en.s6.return-interest.a.result: You arrange a short session for {interest} and tell the people affected by the change. The first attempt is uneven; you keep it anyway.
en.s6.return-interest.a.follow: You have tried again on a few ordinary evenings. Some weeks you miss it. There is now an actual new piece beside the work you put away.
en.s6.return-interest.a.later: Years later, you compare the two pieces. You still have work to do and things you cannot do yet; beginning again did not require becoming someone else.
en.s6.return-interest.b.result: You attend an introductory activity and ask a beginner question. You leave with one idea to try at home, without signing up for a new life plan.
en.s6.return-interest.b.follow: You try the idea at home. It takes less equipment than you feared and more patience than you expected. This one experiment is yours.
en.s6.return-interest.b.later: Years later, the note from that visit is still among your things. You have not made this a career; you did learn one thing you had wanted to know.
en.s6.return-interest.c: Keep the materials; choose rest today
en.s6.return-interest.c.result: You put the materials somewhere you can find them and choose a quiet evening. You do not owe the invitation a yes.
en.s6.return-interest.c.follow: You see the materials again while tidying. They are still available; the quiet evening you chose was real, too.
en.s6.return-interest.c.later: Years later, you recognize the decision as a limit you needed then. The record keeps an interest open without inventing practice that never happened.
en.s6.family-time: What would count as being here?
en.s6.family-time.prompt: {person} is part of your present life, not a deadline. You have work and limits of your own. What time could you offer without promising more than you can give?
en.s6.family-time.setup: In an ordinary exchange with {person}, a small family story comes up. Work has been taking much of your attention. You make a note of the story rather than calling a visit already arranged.
en.s6.family-time.a.result: You and {person} agree on a small time together and move one optional plan. During it, you ask about the family story and listen past the first answer.
en.s6.family-time.a.follow: You and {person} revisit a detail from that time. What remains is not a perfect family portrait, but one conversation you actually made room for.
en.s6.family-time.a.later: Years later, you can tell the small story more clearly because you asked. You keep what was actually said, without claiming one visit repaired everything.
en.s6.family-time.b: Offer a shorter conversation I can sustain
en.s6.family-time.b.result: You tell {person} how much time you can offer and share a short conversation. You listen carefully instead of apologizing through the whole exchange.
en.s6.family-time.b.follow: You remember one thing {person} said in that short exchange. Its length did not prevent it from being a real shared moment.
en.s6.family-time.b.later: Years later, you can place that sentence in an ordinary day. Being present then had a modest, possible size.
en.s6.family-time.c: Explain my limits and leave the plan open
en.s6.family-time.c.result: You tell {person} that you cannot arrange time now and avoid promising an uncertain date. The family story remains a note, not a completed visit.
en.s6.family-time.c.follow: You reread the note and remember why you left the plan open. No visit is added to the record; neither is a punishment for needing limits.
en.s6.family-time.c.later: Years later, the unfinished plan is still distinguishable from the times you did share. You can hold both gratitude and an unanswered question.
en.s6.work-boundary: What can you promise this time
en.s6.work-boundary.prompt: Helping is possible, but the extra time would come from your own plans. How much can you honestly offer?
en.s6.work-boundary.preludeTitle: Another request at the end of the day
en.s6.work-boundary.setup: At work, you receive a request to help beyond the task you had agreed to finish. You have already completed your planned work.
en.s6.work-boundary.a: Help this time, with a clear stopping point
en.s6.work-boundary.a.result: You offer a limited amount of help and name the stopping point. A personal plan is shortened.
en.s6.work-boundary.a.follow: You complete the agreed part of the help. Naming its limit keeps this one request from becoming an unlimited promise.
en.s6.work-boundary.b: Discuss what can wait until another day
en.s6.work-boundary.b.result: You explain your availability and help separate the urgent part from what can wait.
en.s6.work-boundary.b.follow: The work is divided into smaller commitments. Negotiating the request becomes part of doing the work well.
en.s6.work-boundary.c: Decline and keep the original plans
en.s6.work-boundary.c.result: You decline the extra request politely. Someone else will need to arrange that work; your personal time remains yours.
en.s6.work-boundary.c.follow: You remember one occasion when you kept a boundary without needing to turn the other person into a villain.
en.s6.shared-time: Make room for the two of you
en.s6.shared-time.prompt: You can name a small thing to do together, rather than waiting for a perfect free week. What would you like to propose?
en.s6.shared-time.preludeTitle: A plan you wrote down together
en.s6.shared-time.setup: You and {person} write down one small thing you would like to do together. It is a plan, not yet a shared outing.
en.s6.shared-time.a: Set aside time for the original plan
en.s6.shared-time.a.result: You and {person} set aside time and complete the small plan. Another optional activity is left for later.
en.s6.shared-time.a.follow: You now share a memory of doing the thing, instead of only talking about doing it someday.
en.s6.shared-time.b: Suggest a simpler version for today
en.s6.shared-time.b.result: You and {person} choose a simpler version and do it together. The larger plan is still open.
en.s6.shared-time.b.follow: You remember that an ordinary shared hour could count without being a perfect occasion.
en.s6.shared-time.c: Talk about why the plan keeps slipping
en.s6.shared-time.c.result: You and {person} talk about what has been taking your attention. You do not record an outing that has not happened.
en.s6.shared-time.c.follow: You have a clearer conversation to refer to when deciding what to arrange next.
en.s6.friend-repair: Leave it there, or try another sentence
en.s6.friend-repair.prompt: You remember both the awkward exchange and the earlier years you shared with {person}. What would be honest to do next?
en.s6.friend-repair.preludeTitle: A message that felt harder to answer
en.s6.friend-repair.setup: In a conversation you renewed with {person}, one short exchange ends awkwardly. You leave it unanswered for now.
en.s6.friend-repair.a: Explain what I meant and leave space for a reply
en.s6.friend-repair.a.result: You explain one thing you meant without deciding what {person} must have intended.
en.s6.friend-repair.a.follow: A later reply clears up part of the misunderstanding. Not every difference disappears, but one sentence becomes easier to understand.
en.s6.friend-repair.b: Ask how the exchange felt to them
en.s6.friend-repair.b.result: You ask {person} about the exchange and listen before writing another explanation.
en.s6.friend-repair.b.follow: You learn a detail about how the conversation landed. Listening changes what you choose to say next.
en.s6.friend-repair.c.result: You choose not to send another message now. The disagreement is not recorded as resolved.
en.s6.friend-repair.c.follow: You remember choosing space. The record keeps the unanswered part rather than inventing a reconciliation.
en.s6.later-letter: What would you keep from this chapter
en.s6.later-letter.prompt: You can write about a choice you made, something you learned, or an ordinary moment worth keeping. Where would you begin?
en.s6.later-letter.preludeTitle: A page for someone still learning
en.s6.later-letter.setup: You set aside a page to write about an experience you actually lived through, without turning it into advice for everyone.
en.s6.later-letter.a: Write honestly about a difficult choice
en.s6.later-letter.a.result: You write about an earlier recorded choice, including what you could not know at the time.
en.s6.later-letter.a.follow: The page gives your earlier self some context instead of judging the choice only by what came afterward.
en.s6.later-letter.b: Keep an ordinary moment in detail
en.s6.later-letter.b.result: You describe one earlier recorded moment, keeping the small details rather than claiming a grand lesson.
en.s6.later-letter.b.follow: You can return to a particular scene from this life, not only a list of achievements.
en.s6.later-letter.c: Leave a page open and keep the record
en.s6.later-letter.c.result: You leave the page open and keep the earlier record. Today you do not need to finish interpreting your life.
en.s6.later-letter.c.follow: The open page remains part of the collection. You can keep a life without reducing it to one lesson.
en.s6.memory-box: Choose a first page for the collection
en.s6.memory-box.prompt: There is no need to know how the rest of life will unfold. Looking at what has already happened, how would you begin telling this story?
en.s6.memory-box.setup: You gather a few records from this life: things you chose and moments you decided to keep.
en.s6.memory-box.a.result: You place an earlier choice at the beginning of the collection, keeping its actual outcome beside it.
en.s6.memory-box.a.follow: The collection now begins with a decision in context. It does not claim that one choice explains your whole life.
en.s6.memory-box.b: Begin with an ordinary moment I kept
en.s6.memory-box.b.result: You place a recorded moment at the beginning. The smaller scene is allowed to matter.
en.s6.memory-box.b.follow: Your collection leaves room for what was lived, alongside what could be measured.
en.s6.memory-box.c: Keep the chapters in the order they happened
en.s6.memory-box.c.result: You keep the recorded order instead of choosing one event to stand for everything.
en.s6.memory-box.c.follow: The collection remains a sequence of chapters, with room for mixed feelings and unfinished questions.

en.s6.SGP.return.c.follow: You see the materials again while tidying. They are still available; the quiet evening you chose was real, too.
en.s6.SGP.return.c.later: Years later, you recognize the decision as a limit you needed then. The record keeps an interest open without inventing practice that never happened.
en.s6.SGP.visit: What would count as being here?
en.s6.SGP.visit.prompt: {person} is part of your present life, not a deadline. You have work and limits of your own. What time could you offer without promising more than you can give? The starting point is recording the explanation of a photograph in the words used at home, not an obligation to follow a cultural script.
en.s6.SGP.visit.setup: During recording the explanation of a photograph in the words used at home, {person} mentions a detail you had never asked about. Work has filled your days. You note the question without pretending you have already made time.
en.s6.SGP.visit.a.result: You and {person} agree on a small time together and move one optional plan. During it, you ask about the family story and listen past the first answer.
en.s6.SGP.visit.a.follow: You and {person} revisit a detail from that time. What remains is not a perfect family portrait, but one conversation you actually made room for.
en.s6.SGP.visit.a.later: Years later, you can tell the small story more clearly because you asked. You keep what was actually said, without claiming one visit repaired everything.
en.s6.SGP.visit.b: Offer a shorter conversation I can sustain
en.s6.SGP.visit.b.result: You tell {person} how much time you can offer and share a short conversation. You listen carefully instead of apologizing through the whole exchange.
en.s6.SGP.visit.b.follow: You remember one thing {person} said in that short exchange. Its length did not prevent it from being a real shared moment.
en.s6.SGP.visit.b.later: Years later, you can place that sentence in an ordinary day. Being present then had a modest, possible size.
en.s6.SGP.visit.c: Explain my limits and leave the plan open
en.s6.SGP.visit.c.result: You tell {person} that you cannot arrange time now and avoid promising an uncertain date. The family story remains a note, not a completed visit.
en.s6.SGP.visit.c.follow: You reread the note and remember why you left the plan open. No visit is added to the record; neither is a punishment for needing limits.
en.s6.SGP.visit.c.later: Years later, the unfinished plan is still distinguishable from the times you did share. You can hold both gratitude and an unanswered question.
